analysis.one_liner: Taxes billionaires on their investments every year, ending deferral loopholes like 'buy, borrow, die'.
analysis.headline: The Billionaires Income Tax Act was introduced by Sen. Wyden with 19 Democratic cosponsors on Nov. 30, 2023, and died in the Senate Finance Committee without a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would require households with over $100 million in income or over $1 billion in assets to pay tax on the yearly gains of their investments—even ones they haven't sold—the same way workers pay tax on every paycheck. It also closes loopholes that let the ultrawealthy borrow against untaxed assets, hand assets to heirs tax-free, and dodge tax by renouncing citizenship. The bill was referred to the Senate Finance Committee and never received a hearing, markup, or floor vote before the 118th Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Everyone who pays ordinary income tax on wages. The bill aims to make roughly the wealthiest thousand or so American households pay taxes annually instead of deferring them indefinitely; the revenue could reduce deficits or fund other priorities, easing pressure on other taxpayers.

how_it_helps.text: Requires taxpayers with over $100 million in income or over $1 billion in assets to recognize gains and losses each year on tradable investments as if sold at fair market value, matching how workers are taxed annually on wages.
Taxpayers who leave applicable-taxpayer status and re-enter it must recapture deferred gains plus interest when they sell or transfer nontradable assets.
Requires mark-to-market taxation on shares of gains and losses from pass-through entities like partnerships held by significant-owner taxpayers.
Closes loopholes like the exclusion for certain small business stock and modifies qualified opportunity fund investment rules for these taxpayers.

analysis.who_pays: The wealthiest households: the bill applies only to people with over $100 million in annual income (or $50 million if married filing separately) or over $1 billion in tradable and nontradable covered assets (or $500 million if married filing separately), sustained across three years.

drawbacks.text: Valuing hard-to-price private assets (startups, art, private equity) annually invites disputes, gaming, and heavy reliance on the Treasury Secretary's judgment.
First-year net tax liability on mark-to-market gains can be paid in five equal annual installments, giving the transition some liquidity relief but adding administrative complexity.
Refunds or credits against tax can be accelerated or disallowed in specific scenarios (e.g., misvaluation, failure-to-file notices, death, bankruptcy petitions).
This is the fourth consecutive attempt to tax billionaire unrealized gains; earlier versions stalled too, raising doubts about political feasibility rather than design merit.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The upside is a more level playing field: the wealthiest households would no longer be able to live off borrowing against untaxed gains while workers pay tax every year. The costs fall almost entirely on those same households, though valuation complexity and the fact that this idea has now stalled four times without ever reaching a committee vote are real design and feasibility issues.

outcome.mechanism: Introduced Nov. 30, 2023, read twice, and referred to the Senate Finance Committee, where it sat without a hearing, markup, or floor vote until the 118th Congress ended Jan. 3, 2025.

narrative.text: Sen. Ron Wyden introduced the Billionaires Income Tax Act on Nov. 30, 2023, alongside 16 original cosponsors, all Democrats.
The bill was read twice and referred to the Committee on Finance the same day, its only recorded action beyond introduction.
Final cosponsor count was 19 Democrats (18 of 48 Senate Democrats and 1 of 4 Senate independents), with no Republican cosponsors recorded.
No committee hearing, markup, floor debate, or roll-call vote occurred before the 118th Congress ended Jan. 3, 2025.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The wealthiest households avoided any new tax on unrealized investment gains, since the bill never reached a hearing or vote and died with the 118th Congress. Wealth-management, private-equity, and tax-planning industries also retained the status quo of deferral strategies the bill targeted.

sides.party_line_note: All 19 cosponsors were Democrats or the independent who caucuses with them (18 of 48 Democrats, 1 of 4 independents); no Republican sponsored or cosponsored the bill.

industries.note: Would have to pay tax annually on investment gains instead of deferring indefinitely through strategies like borrowing against unsold assets. Directly targets the top fraction of one percent of households.

industries.industry: Tax, wealth management, and estate-planning services
industries.note: Loophole-closing provisions (like-kind exchange limits, grantor trust rules, small business stock exclusion repeal) would shrink demand for deferral-based tax planning.
Nontradable covered asset rules (deferral recapture, five-year installment elections, and pass-through entity gain reporting) would tax gains currently sheltered until exit.

industries.industry: Real estate and like-kind exchange participants
industries.note: Section 211 modifies treatment of like-kind exchanges by applicable entities, curtailing a deferral tool heavily used in real estate.
